subject: English
source: National Curriculum Year 4 English (fronted adverbials, speech punctuation, possessive apostrophes, Standard English, narrative writing); Drive English folder held no KS2 material so content is original

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Punctuation and grammar for stronger writing
lessons.title: Fronted adverbials and commas
objectives: Identify fronted adverbials of time, place and manner
Punctuate a fronted adverbial with a comma

keywords.def: a word or phrase that tells us when, where or how something happens
an adverbial placed at the start of a sentence
a punctuation mark that separates parts of a sentence
a group of words containing a verb

starter: Say bismillah. Underline the adverb: The boy ran quickly.
Write a sentence using because.
Add inverted commas: Come here, said Hana.

teach.heading: Adverbials
bullets: Adverbials tell us when, where or how
They can be one word or a phrase
after lunch, in the garden, with great care
teach.note: Begin by revising adverbs from Year 3. Explain that an adverbial can be a phrase. Show 'We played football after lunch.' Ask where the adverbial is. Then show it at the front.

teach.heading: Moving it to the front
bullets: The comma shows where the adverbial ends
teach.note: Demonstrate moving the adverbial. Point out that the meaning stays the same, but the sentence opening changes. Introduce the term fronted adverbial and the rule: put a comma after it.

teach.heading: Three types
teach.note: Give each type a colour. Show examples and ask pupils to sort cards. Include 'Suddenly,' as a one-word adverbial. Misconception: pupils forget the comma after short adverbials.

teach.heading: Why use them?
bullets: They give clear information to the reader
They help show time passing in stories
teach.note: Show a paragraph where every sentence begins with 'He'. Rewrite with fronted adverbials. Ask which version reads better and why.

teach.heading: Check your punctuation
teach.note: Model checking three sentences. Pupils write on mini-whiteboards: 'In the playground, ...' and hold up their sentences. Check for the comma.

practice: Add a comma: Early in the morning the baker lit the oven.
Move the adverbial to the front: We prayed in the mosque.
Is this time, place or manner: Under the old bridge,
independent: Write ten sentences beginning with fronted adverbials (time, place and manner) about a day out.
Rewrite five sentences by moving the adverbial to the front, adding commas.
Underline the fronted adverbials in a short paragraph provided by your teacher.
exit: Write a sentence with a fronted adverbial of place.
Where does the comma go in: Without a sound the cat crept away.
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph about your journey to school using four fronted adverbials.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence cards with commas to add. EAL: practise with picture prompts and sentence frames. Stretch: use two fronted adverbials in one sentence.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Punctuation and grammar for stronger writing
lessons.title: Punctuating direct speech
objectives: Punctuate direct speech with inverted commas and commas
Place end punctuation inside inverted commas

keywords.def: the actual words someone says
marks around spoken words
words showing who is speaking and how
a different person talking, who needs a new line

starter: Bismillah. Add a comma: Later that day we visited the market.
Name a fronted adverbial of place.
What is a verb? Give two.

teach.heading: Direct speech
bullets: The exact words a person says
Use inverted commas around the speech
teach.note: Ask two pupils to say a short sentence. Write exactly what they said, using inverted commas. Revise from Year 3.

teach.heading: Speech first
bullets: Comma inside the closing inverted commas
Reporting clause starts with a lower-case letter
teach.note: Model carefully. The spoken words begin with a capital letter. The comma comes before the closing inverted commas. The reporting clause begins with a small letter unless it is a name.

teach.heading: Reporting clause first
bullets: Full stop inside the inverted commas
teach.note: Contrast with the previous slide. When the reporting clause comes first, a comma follows it. The spoken words begin with a capital letter. Misconception: forgetting the comma after said.

teach.heading: Questions and exclamations
bullets: End mark stays inside the speech marks
teach.note: Explain that a question mark or exclamation mark replaces the comma. The reporting clause still begins with a lower-case letter. Read aloud with expression.

teach.heading: New speaker, new line
bullets: Every new speaker begins a new line
Add action to show who is speaking
Check all marks are in place
teach.note: Show a short conversation without lines and ask pupils to rewrite with new lines. Use real examples such as a conversation at the shop. Praise tidy punctuation.

practice: Punctuate: I am ready said Zaid
Punctuate: Sara asked Can we go now
Rewrite so the reporting clause comes first: "Hurry up!" shouted Dad.
independent: Punctuate ten sentences of speech correctly.
Write a conversation of eight lines between a shopkeeper and a customer.
Add a reporting clause with an adverb, for example said quietly.
exit: Punctuate: Stop shouted the guard
Where does the comma go when the reporting clause comes first?
lessons.homework: Write a conversation between two friends planning a picnic. Use at least four lines of speech.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a speech punctuation checklist. EAL: use speech bubbles then convert to inverted commas. Stretch: write speech split by a reporting clause.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Punctuation and grammar for stronger writing
lessons.title: Possessive apostrophes
objectives: Use apostrophes to show singular possession
Use apostrophes for plural possession, including irregular plurals

keywords.def: a mark (') that shows possession or missing letters
when something belongs to someone
one
more than one

starter: Bismillah. Write the plural: box, child, baby.
Punctuate: Come here said Mum.
Write a fronted adverbial of time.

teach.heading: What is possession?
teach.note: Show a picture of a coat and ask whose it is. Write 'the coat of the boy' then 'the boy's coat'. Explain that the apostrophe shows ownership.

teach.heading: One owner
teach.note: Practise with items in the room. Model with a name that ends in s: James's book (or James' book, either accepted in school). Warn about the common mistake of putting an apostrophe in plurals: apple's.

teach.heading: Many owners, plural with s
bullets: Add the apostrophe after the s
teach.note: Use a visual to show the difference: boy's (one boy) and boys' (more than one boy). Ask pupils which they would use for 'the books belonging to the girls'. They must decide first whether there is one or many owners.

teach.heading: Irregular plurals
bullets: the women's meeting, the men's coats
teach.note: Remind pupils that children, men, women and mice do not end in s, so 's is added. Show 'the childrens toys' is wrong and 'the children's toys' is right.

teach.heading: Test: who owns it?
bullets: Many owners ending in s: after s
teach.note: Give a quick-fire round. Show 'the dog's bones' (one dog) and 'the dogs' bones' (many). Check pupils understand the order of letters.

practice: Add the apostrophe: the cats bowl (one cat)
Add the apostrophe: the girls bags (more than one girl)
Correct: the childrens playground
independent: Rewrite ten phrases using an apostrophe (e.g. the hat of the king).
Write six sentences using possessive apostrophes.
Find the mistakes in a short paragraph and correct them.
exit: Which is correct: the boys' ball or the boy's ball (two boys)?
Write the possessive for the toys belonging to the children.
lessons.homework: Look for five examples of apostrophes for possession at home and write what they show.
lessons.send: SEND: use a one/many owner sorting sheet. EAL: practise with objects and pictures. Stretch: explain the difference between the dogs' and the dog's bowls.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Punctuation and grammar for stronger writing
lessons.title: Standard English verb forms
objectives: Use Standard English verb forms in writing
Correct non-standard forms such as we was and I done

keywords.def: the form of English used in formal writing and speech
the way a verb changes for tense and person
who or what does the action
shows an action that has happened

starter: Bismillah. Add an apostrophe: the teachers book.
Write the past tense of: go, see, do.
Write a sentence using a fronted adverbial.

teach.heading: Spoken and written English
bullets: We often speak in a relaxed way
teach.note: Explain that there is nothing wrong with our home or local ways of speaking, but formal writing follows Standard English. Ask when a different style of language might be needed: a letter, a news report.

teach.heading: was and were
bullets: I was, he was, she was, it was
we were, you were, they were
Wrong: we was; right: we were
teach.note: Chant the forms. Show errors in sentences and ask pupils to correct them. Misconception: 'they was'. Use cards for quick practice.

teach.heading: did, done and seen, saw
bullets: I saw a rainbow; I have seen a rainbow
teach.note: Contrast simple past with the perfect form from Year 3. Wrong: 'I done it' and 'I seen it'. Use sentence stems: yesterday I... (did/saw), I have... (done/seen).

teach.heading: Other common errors
bullets: I didn't do anything, not I didn't do nothing
he and I went, not me and him went
teach.note: Cover double negatives. Explain that two negatives cancel each other in Standard English. Keep a friendly tone: we are learning the right tool for the job.

teach.heading: Proofreading for verbs
bullets: Read aloud to hear the error
Check each verb with its subject
teach.note: Provide a sample paragraph with five errors for the class to correct. Use a colour code for corrections. Praise careful reading.

practice: Correct: We was late for school.
Correct: I done my work.
Correct: Them books are heavy.
independent: Rewrite ten sentences in Standard English.
Write a short paragraph about a school trip using was, were, did and saw correctly.
Spot and fix five errors in a short diary entry.
exit: Correct: They was playing outside.
Complete: Yesterday I ___ (see) a hawk.
lessons.homework: Write six sentences in Standard English about last weekend.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence cards with correct and incorrect forms. EAL: focus on was and were with pictures. Stretch: explain why Standard English is used in formal writing.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Punctuation and grammar for stronger writing
lessons.title: Pronouns and cohesion
objectives: Use pronouns to avoid repetition
Make sure it is clear who a pronoun refers to

keywords.def: a word that takes the place of a noun, such as he, she, it, they
how the parts of a text link together
using the same word too often
to point back to something

starter: Bismillah. Correct: We was happy.
Add an apostrophe: the girls coats (many girls).
Move the adverbial to the front: He came home at noon.

teach.heading: What is a pronoun?
bullets: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
Sinbad found an egg. He found an egg.
teach.note: Show a repetitive paragraph: 'Sinbad woke. Sinbad looked around. Sinbad was alone.' Ask what sounds odd and improve with he.

teach.heading: Choose pronouns carefully
bullets: Use a noun at first, then a pronoun
Sinbad saw the roc. He was amazed.
teach.note: Model the pattern: noun first, then pronoun. Explain that readers must know who 'he' is. Introduce possessive pronouns: his, her, their.

teach.heading: Ambiguous pronouns
bullets: Sinbad told the merchant he was brave.
Fix: Sinbad told the merchant, "You are brave."
teach.note: Discuss unclear references. Ask pupils to rewrite so the meaning is clear. Misconception: more pronouns always make writing better.

teach.heading: Nouns across sentences
bullets: The roc flapped her wings. The giant bird rose.
teach.note: Show that a new noun phrase can refer back to the same thing: the roc, the giant bird, the huge creature. This avoids repetition and adds detail.

teach.heading: Improve a paragraph
bullets: Replace with pronouns or noun phrases
teach.note: Provide a paragraph to improve together. Take suggestions on the board and ask pupils to explain their choices.

practice: Replace with a pronoun: Layla opened the door. Layla smiled.
Who does 'they' refer to: Omar and Sami ran. They stopped.
Write a noun phrase for a lion to avoid repeating the word.
independent: Rewrite a paragraph about a merchant to remove repetition.
Fix four unclear sentences.
Write a short paragraph about a market using nouns and pronouns clearly.
exit: Replace the repeated noun with a pronoun: The ship sailed. The ship was fast.
Why can a pronoun be confusing?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph about a character using pronouns and noun phrases carefully.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight the repeated nouns in colour. EAL: provide a pronoun table. Stretch: write a paragraph with three different ways to refer to the same character.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Sinbad and the roc - reading and writing an adventure
lessons.title: Reading the adventure: Sinbad and the roc
objectives: Read a story and retrieve key facts
Summarise the main events in order

keywords.def: an exciting story with danger and risk
find information in a text
a short account of the main points
the order of events

starter: Bismillah. Replace with a pronoun: Sinbad was clever. Sinbad escaped.
Write a fronted adverbial of time.
Punctuate: Look shouted Sinbad.

teach.heading: Sinbad the Sailor
bullets: Each voyage brings danger and a clever escape
teach.note: Introduce Sinbad as a character from the collection of stories known as One Thousand and One Nights. Explain that today's version is a retelling. Ask pupils what they know about adventures at sea.

teach.heading: Read the story
bullets: Sinbad is left on an island
The roc carries him to a valley of diamonds
Merchants and eagles help him escape
teach.note: Sinbad woke to find that his ship had sailed without him. He was alone on a deserted island. Wandering inland, he came upon an enormous white dome, as smooth as marble. It was the egg of a giant bird called the roc! Suddenly, the sky grew dark as the roc returned to her nest. Sinbad was quick-witted. He unwound his turban and tied himself to one of her huge legs. At dawn, the bird soared into the sky and carried him across the sea. She landed in a deep valley where the ground sparkled with diamonds. But the valley was full of huge, hissing snakes! Sinbad hid in a cave until he saw merchants on the cliffs above hurling lumps of meat into the valley. Diamonds stuck to the meat, and eagles swooped down to carry it away. Sinbad filled his pockets with diamonds, strapped a piece of meat to his back and was lifted out of danger. Read aloud with drama, stopping after the egg to predict what happens.

teach.heading: Retrieving facts
teach.note: Model finding the answer to 'What was the egg like?' (as smooth as marble). Show how to underline the key words and use them in an answer.

teach.heading: Sequence the story
bullets: First: the ship sails without Sinbad
Next: he finds the egg and the roc
Then: the valley and the snakes
teach.note: Use time adverbials to order events. Ask pupils to retell the story in four sentences using a different time word each time.

teach.heading: Summarising
teach.note: Model a two-sentence summary. Check that the summary avoids detail such as the colour of the dome. Pupils write their summary on mini-whiteboards.

practice: Who or what is the roc?
How did Sinbad travel to the valley?
What lay on the ground of the valley?
independent: Answer six retrieval questions in full sentences.
Put eight events in order.
Write a four-sentence summary of the story.
exit: How did Sinbad escape from the valley?
Write one time adverbial you used in your summary.
lessons.homework: Retell the story in your own words to an adult, using at least three time words.
lessons.send: SEND: sequence cards with pictures. EAL: pre-teach deserted, enormous, soared. Stretch: write the story from the roc's viewpoint in three sentences.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Sinbad and the roc - reading and writing an adventure
lessons.title: Vocabulary in context and words ending -ous
objectives: Work out word meanings using context and root words
Spell words ending in -ous

keywords.def: the words around a word that help show its meaning
the main part of a word
a suffix meaning full of, as in dangerous
a book or tool that lists words with similar meanings

starter: Bismillah. Write the plural possessive: the merchants (ship).
Write a summary of the story in one sentence.
What is a pronoun?

teach.heading: Find the meaning
bullets: Read the sentence before and after
teach.note: Model with 'deserted': 'alone on a deserted island'. What clue helps? 'Alone' tells us nobody is there. Show how to try a replacement word and reread.

teach.heading: Key words from the text
bullets: quick-witted = clever and fast to think
teach.note: Pupils match words to meanings and use them in spoken sentences. Ask what other word could replace 'huge' in the story.

teach.heading: Words ending in -ous
teach.note: -ous means 'full of'. Explain the spelling rules: most words just add -ous; with a final e, sometimes the e drops (fame - famous) and sometimes it stays (courage - courageous). Learn the common ones.

teach.heading: Synonyms and a thesaurus
bullets: Choose the one that fits best
teach.note: Explain shades of meaning: 'huge' is bigger than 'large'. Use a thesaurus. Warn: check meaning in context, not just any word from a list.

teach.heading: Use new words
teach.note: Take pupil sentences. Praise accurate, imaginative usage. Link to appreciating Allah's creation when describing wonders in nature.

practice: What does 'hurling' mean in the sentence?
Spell: dangerous, famous.
Give a synonym for 'huge'.
independent: Match eight words to their meanings.
Write six sentences using words from the story.
Add -ous to five root words and spell them correctly.
exit: Spell the word meaning 'full of adventure'.
Choose a synonym for 'soared'.
lessons.homework: Learn to spell: dangerous, famous, enormous, adventurous, mountainous.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards with images. EAL: use bilingual dictionaries for key words. Stretch: group words by shade of meaning and explain your order.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Sinbad and the roc - reading and writing an adventure
lessons.title: Character, inference and explaining our views
objectives: Infer what Sinbad is like from his actions
Support answers with evidence

keywords.def: work out something using clues
words from the text that prove an idea
a quality that a character shows, such as bravery
copy exact words from a text

starter: Bismillah. Spell: enormous, adventurous, famous.
What does 'soared' mean?
Write one synonym for 'clever'.

teach.heading: Inference
bullets: We work out meaning from clues
teach.note: Show a picture of a child with a frown and ask what they might feel. Link to inference: we use clues when authors do not tell us directly.

teach.heading: What is Sinbad like?
bullets: Quick-witted: he ties himself to the roc
Resourceful: he uses meat to escape
teach.note: Reread parts of the story. Ask which words show each quality. Model a full answer with quote: 'Sinbad is quick-witted because he unwound his turban and tied himself to the roc's leg.'

teach.heading: Using quotes
teach.note: Model embedding: Sinbad is clever because he 'unwound his turban'. Explain that we copy exactly. Pupils practise adding short quotes to their answers.

teach.heading: Fact and feeling
bullets: How might Sinbad feel in the valley?
teach.note: Ask pupils to consider his feelings from the situation, not only from words used. 'Hissing snakes' makes the scene threatening. Ask them to justify.

teach.heading: Writing your answer
teach.note: Model a three-part answer. Provide a sentence frame: 'I think..., because the text says '...'. This shows that...'.

practice: Find a word or phrase that shows Sinbad was clever.
How do you think Sinbad felt when he saw the snakes? Why?
What does the phrase 'hid in a cave' show?
independent: Write three P.E.E. paragraphs about Sinbad's qualities.
Find two quotes that show danger.
Write a comparison: Sinbad at the start and end of the extract.
exit: Complete: Sinbad is brave because...
Write a quote that shows the valley was dangerous.
lessons.homework: Write a short character profile of Sinbad with evidence.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight evidence in the text and give frames. EAL: use word banks for qualities. Stretch: consider whether the merchants or Sinbad are more resourceful.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Sinbad and the roc - reading and writing an adventure
lessons.title: Writing a setting description
objectives: Use the senses to describe a setting
Use fronted adverbials, similes and noun phrases in description

keywords.def: where and when a story takes place
compares one thing to another using like or as
sight, sound, smell, touch, taste
the feeling a setting creates

starter: Bismillah. Write a sentence with a fronted adverbial of place.
Write an expanded noun phrase about a cave.
What is a simile?

teach.heading: What is a setting?
bullets: Where and when the story happens
Good description helps readers picture the scene
teach.note: Show a picture of a valley sparkling with diamonds and snakes among the rocks. Ask pupils how they would feel there. Link the setting to the mood: wonder and danger.

teach.heading: Use the senses
teach.note: Collect words for each sense. Model a sentence combining two senses: 'In the shadows, hissing snakes slithered over the cold, rough rocks.'

teach.heading: Similes
bullets: The valley sparkled like a sky full of stars.
teach.note: Explain that a good simile helps the reader imagine. Avoid clichés. Ask for fresh comparisons. Check there is a real similarity: 'sparkling like a sea of stars'.

teach.heading: Build a paragraph
teach.note: Model the paragraph: 'At the bottom of the valley, a carpet of glittering diamonds sparkled like frost in the sun. Beyond the rocks, hissing snakes coiled and uncoiled.' Underline the features.

teach.heading: Check it works
bullets: Have I used commas after fronted adverbials?
teach.note: Display a checklist and ask pupils to review their partner's sentences. Praise vivid, accurate phrases.

practice: Write one sentence describing the sound in the valley.
Complete the simile: The snakes were as long as...
Add a fronted adverbial: ____, the diamonds glittered.
independent: Write a paragraph describing the valley of diamonds using at least three senses.
Include a simile and two fronted adverbials.
Underline your best phrase.
exit: Write a simile for the roc's wings.
Which sense have you used most?
lessons.homework: Write a description of a place you know using three senses.
lessons.send: SEND: sense word bank and picture. EAL: label the picture first. Stretch: use a metaphor as well as a simile.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Sinbad and the roc - reading and writing an adventure
lessons.title: Planning our own voyage
objectives: Plan a new adventure episode in paragraphs
Choose a problem and clever solution

keywords.def: the events of a story
a group of sentences about one idea or event
the danger or challenge
how the character solves the problem

starter: Bismillah. Name two senses you use in description.
Write a simile about a mountain.
Punctuate: Help cried Sinbad.

teach.heading: An adventure plot
teach.note: Share a simple structure. Link each part to the story we read. Note that the problem should be solved by cleverness and courage, not just luck.

teach.heading: Our setting and danger
bullets: Choose a place: island, cave, desert
Choose a danger: storm, giant, beast
teach.note: Brainstorm in pairs. Collect ideas on the board. Warn pupils to keep the ideas realistic within the fantasy: the solution must use something Sinbad has or can find.

teach.heading: Plan in paragraphs
teach.note: Show a four-box plan. Explain that each paragraph deals with one stage and starts with a fronted adverbial. Model a plan: a desert storm, a hidden well, a camel caravan.

teach.heading: Plan the language
bullets: A fronted adverbial for each paragraph
teach.note: Model planning vocabulary: 'swirling sand', 'howling wind'. Ask pupils to choose three powerful words for each paragraph.

teach.heading: Share and improve
bullets: Tell your plan to a partner
Does the problem need a clever solution?
teach.note: Pairs share. Partner gives one star and one suggestion. Link to adab of listening: let your partner finish before responding.

practice: Choose your setting and danger.
Write a fronted adverbial for the start of your story.
Write the problem in one sentence.
independent: Complete a four-paragraph plan.
Write a list of ten powerful words for your story.
Write two lines of speech for your plan.
exit: State your problem and solution in two sentences.
Which paragraph will include dialogue?
lessons.homework: Improve your plan by adding detail to the solution.
lessons.send: SEND: use a plan with sentence starters. EAL: draw the four stages before writing. Stretch: add a surprise or twist in paragraph 3.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Sinbad and the roc - reading and writing an adventure
lessons.title: Writing our adventure
objectives: Write an adventure in paragraphs
Use punctuation learnt in this unit accurately

keywords.def: a first version of writing
a group of sentences about one idea or event
words spoken by characters
a feeling of suspense or worry

starter: Bismillah. Punctuate: Hurry shouted Sinbad.
Add a comma: Without a sound the beast crept closer.
Write a pronoun for Sinbad.

teach.heading: Start strongly
teach.note: Model an opening: 'Early one morning, Sinbad's ship reached a golden island of sand dunes and silent palm trees.' Write alongside pupils.

teach.heading: Build tension
teach.note: Model: 'Suddenly, the ground shook. Sinbad froze.' Compare with a long sentence. Ask what effect short sentences create.

teach.heading: Include dialogue
teach.note: Model speech that moves the story on. Pupils write one line. Remind them to use varied reporting clauses.

teach.heading: Use cohesion
teach.note: Revisit lesson 5. Ask pupils to check that it is clear who each pronoun means. Show a sample paragraph where Sinbad is replaced by 'the sailor' and 'the young merchant'.

teach.heading: Write and review
bullets: Write your story over two stages
teach.note: Pupils draft paragraphs 1 and 2 first. Circulate and give feedback on punctuation. Remind them to check commas and apostrophes.

practice: Write your first sentence with a fronted adverbial.
Write a line of speech with correct punctuation.
Write a short sentence to show danger.
independent: Write paragraphs one to three of your adventure.
Include at least one simile and one line of speech.
Underline all fronted adverbials.
exit: Which of your sentences builds tension?
Check one piece of punctuation in your writing.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a writing frame and word bank. EAL: allow oral rehearsal first. Stretch: use a range of sentence lengths to control pace.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Sinbad and the roc - reading and writing an adventure
lessons.title: Editing and improving our writing
objectives: Proofread for Unit 1 skills
Improve vocabulary and share the finished story

keywords.def: check writing for errors
improve writing
helpful comments
produce a neat final version

starter: Bismillah. Correct: We was late.
Add an apostrophe: the childrens boat.
Spell: dangerous, enormous.

teach.heading: The editing checklist
teach.note: Display the list. Model checking one paragraph, showing how to tick, fix and improve. Use a purple pen for corrections.

teach.heading: Improve vocabulary
teach.note: Show a draft sentence and improve it step by step. Demonstrate using a thesaurus carefully. Explain that vocabulary should fit the context.

teach.heading: Peer feedback
teach.note: Model feedback sentences. Link to adab: speak kindly and honestly, and thank your partner for helpful comments.

teach.heading: Reading aloud
bullets: Pause at commas and full stops
teach.note: Practise reading a paragraph with expression. Explain that reading aloud helps us hear missing words and awkward sentences.

teach.heading: Publish and celebrate
bullets: Share the best part with the class
teach.note: Invite volunteers to read their favourite sentence. Praise effort. End with a reflection on what pupils have improved this half term.

practice: Correct: Without a sound the snake slid away.
Add the apostrophe: the sailors ship (one sailor).
Replace 'big' with a stronger adjective.
independent: Edit your adventure with the checklist.
Improve five sentences with better vocabulary.
Write a neat final copy of one paragraph.
exit: Name one punctuation mark you corrected.
Write the title of your story.
lessons.homework: Practise reading your best paragraph aloud.
lessons.send: SEND: use a simplified checklist and tick boxes. EAL: focus on checking one feature at a time. Stretch: rewrite the opening in a different style.
